## Ground lenses `lenses`
- Deps: helped by glassmaking, clear_glass, refraction_optics
- Core idea: A piece of clear glass with spherically curved faces bends light. A convex lens (thicker in the middle) gathers sunlight to a point at its focal length, magnifies near objects and throws an inverted image on a wall; a concave lens (thinner in the middle) spreads light and makes things look smaller. A lens is made by grinding a glass blank against a curved metal dish or ball with wet abrasive (sand, then finer emery) and polishing it with tripoli or rouge on pitch or felt. The flatter the curve, the longer the focal length; for ordinary glass a lens with two equal faces has a focal length about equal to the radius of the curve.
- Pitfalls: Bubbles and streaks scatter or distort light, while a tint mainly reduces transmission; the glass matters as much as the grinding | Thinking lenses were unknown before spectacles: burning glasses and rock-crystal magnifiers are ancient | Skipping the polishing stages: a ground but unpolished surface is matt | Not being able to say what curve is needed (measure the focal length with the sun instead)
- History: mesopotamia: c. 750 BC – Nimrud rock-crystal 'lens' (Assyria); use as a lens is disputed; greece: c. 424 BC – burning glass mentioned in Aristophanes, Clouds; rome: 1st c. AD – Seneca and Pliny describe magnification by water-filled glass globes and burning glasses; islamic: c. 1011–1021 – Ibn al-Haytham, Book of Optics, treats magnification by curved glass; europe: 11th–12th c. rock-crystal Visby lenses; 13th c. reading stones; c. 1286 convex spectacle lenses in Italy; c. 1450 concave lenses; china: rock-crystal burning lenses known by the Han; spectacle lenses arrive from the west in the 15th c.
- Read: Vincent Ilardi, Renaissance Vision from Spectacles to Telescopes (2007) | Henry C. King, The History of the Telescope (1955)

## Spectacles `spectacles`
- Deps: needs lenses
- Core idea: Two lenses in a frame in front of the eyes correct sight. Weak convex lenses help older people who can no longer read close up (almost everyone after about 45); concave lenses help the short-sighted see far. Strength is chosen by trying lenses of graded focal length until small writing is sharp. Reading lenses let scribes and fine craftsmen continue close work as their eyes lose focusing power.
- Pitfalls: Giving convex lenses to a short-sighted person (they make it worse) | Assuming one strength suits everybody or both eyes | Believing spectacles weaken or ruin the eyes (an old and persistent objection)
- History: europe: c. 1286 – convex spectacles made in Pisa or Florence (inventor unknown; Giordano da Pisa's sermon of 1306 dates them); c. 1450 concave lenses for the short-sighted, Florence a main producer; islamic: 14th–15th c. – spectacles known through Italian trade; china: early 15th c. – imported spectacles recorded under the Ming; the claim of a Chinese invention is not supported
- Read: Vincent Ilardi, Renaissance Vision from Spectacles to Telescopes (2007) | Edward Rosen, The Invention of Eyeglasses, Journal of the History of Medicine 11 (1956)

## Law of refraction, image formation and vision `refraction_optics`
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, trigonometry, lenses, camera_obscura
- Core idea: We see because light from the sun or a lamp bounces off things and enters the eye; the eye sends out nothing. Light travels in straight lines, reflects at equal angles, and bends when it passes between air and water or glass: the sine of the angle from the surface normal in air divided by the sine of the angle in the denser medium is a fixed number (about 1.33 for water, about 1.5 for glass). An ideal lens brings rays from one object point to one image point; the eye is such a lens with the retina as the screen, and the image on it is upside down. Cheap demonstrations: a coin at the bottom of a cup comes into view when water is poured in; a stick looks broken at the water surface.
- Pitfalls: Saying the bending angle is simply proportional to the incoming angle (only roughly true for small angles) | Repeating the ancient view that sight goes out from the eye, or accepting it out of politeness | Claiming an upside-down retinal image means we should see the world upside down | Confusing reflection with refraction
- History: greece: c. 300 BC – Euclid, Optics (visual rays leave the eye); c. 160 AD Ptolemy measures refraction in tables, without the sine law; china: c. 4th–3rd c. BC – Mohist Canon on shadows, pinhole images and mirrors; no law of refraction; islamic: c. 984 – Ibn Sahl states a rule equivalent to the sine law; c. 1011–1021 Ibn al-Haytham shows that vision is light entering the eye; europe: 1602 – Harriot finds the sine law (unpublished); 1604 Kepler explains the retinal image; 1621 Snell; 1637 Descartes publishes the law
- Read: Ibn al-Haytham, Kitab al-Manazir (c. 1011–1021; tr. A. I. Sabra, The Optics of Ibn al-Haytham, 1989) | David C. Lindberg, Theories of Vision from al-Kindi to Kepler (1976) | A. Mark Smith, From Sight to Light: The Passage from Ancient to Modern Optics (2015)

## Camera obscura `camera_obscura`
- Deps: helped by lenses
- Core idea: In a darkened room with one small hole in the shutter, the sunlit scene outside appears on the opposite wall, upside down and reversed, in colour and in motion. It works because light travels in straight lines. A smaller hole gives a sharper but dimmer picture; a convex lens in a larger hole gives a bright, sharp picture at its focal distance. It shows how the eye works, lets one watch a solar eclipse or sunspots safely, and lets a draughtsman trace a view in true perspective.
- Pitfalls: Hole too large (blur) or room not fully dark | Forgetting that the image is inverted and promising an upright picture | Looking at the sun through the hole instead of at the projected image
- History: china: c. 4th c. BC – Mohist Canon describes the inverted pinhole image; 1088 Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays; greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotelian Problems note crescent sun images under trees during an eclipse; islamic: c. 1011–1021 – Ibn al-Haytham experiments with the dark chamber and writes On the Shape of the Eclipse; europe: 13th c. used for solar eclipses; c. 1500 Leonardo's notes; 1550 Cardano and 1568 Barbaro add a lens and diaphragm; 1558 and 1589 della Porta popularises it
- Read: John H. Hammond, The Camera Obscura: A Chronicle (1981) | Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 1: Physics (1962)

## Microscope `microscope`
- Deps: needs lenses; helped by clear_glass
- Core idea: The simple microscope is one tiny, strongly curved lens: a glass bead 1–2 mm across, made by melting the end of a drawn glass thread or ground from a chip, set in a hole in a metal plate. Held almost touching the eye, with the object on a pin about a millimetre behind it and strong light from behind, it magnifies 100 to over 250 times, enough to see the living creatures in pond water, in vinegar and in the scrapings from teeth. The compound microscope uses two lenses in a tube (a small objective near the specimen and an eyepiece); until better lenses came in the 19th century it was more convenient but showed less.
- Pitfalls: Using spectacle lenses (far too weak) or expecting the compound form to be better from the start | Poor lighting and thick specimens: the object must be thin and lit from behind | Promising that plague or smallpox agents will be visible (viruses are not; most bacteria need 200 times or more and practice) | Wrong focus distance: the bead lens must be about a millimetre from the object
- History: europe: c. 1590–1620 – compound microscope in the Netherlands (Janssen's claim is doubtful; Drebbel shows one by 1620); 1625 the name 'microscopio' (Accademia dei Lincei); 1665 Hooke, Micrographia; 1674–1683 Leeuwenhoek sees protozoa and bacteria with single lenses; 1830 Lister's achromatic objectives; china: 17th c. – brought by Jesuits
- Read: Robert Hooke, Micrographia (1665) | Brian J. Ford, Single Lens: The Story of the Simple Microscope (1985) | Laura J. Snyder, Eye of the Beholder (2015)

## Telescope (refractor) `telescope`
- Deps: needs lenses; helped by clear_glass, refraction_optics
- Core idea: A weak convex lens of long focal length at the front (objective) and a strong lens of short focal length at the eye, held in a tube that can slide to focus. With a concave eyepiece (Dutch or Galilean form) the image is upright and the tube length is the difference of the two focal lengths; with a convex eyepiece (Kepler's form) it is inverted, the field is wider and the length is the sum. The magnification is the objective's focal length divided by the eyepiece's: a spectacle lens focusing at 1 m with an eyepiece of 5 cm gives 20 times. Covering the outer part of the objective with a ring of card sharpens the image. Twenty times shows Jupiter's four moons, the mountains of the Moon, the phases of Venus and ships hours before the naked eye.
- Pitfalls: Two lenses of similar strength give no magnification | Ordinary spectacle glass is too poor at more than a few times; Galileo ground his own and rejected most lenses | Colour fringes and blur grow with lens diameter; not stopping down the objective | Looking at the Sun through it (blinds); project the image on paper instead | Crediting Galileo with the invention
- History: europe: 1608 – Lipperhey applies for a patent in The Hague (Metius and Janssen also claim it); 1609 Harriot and Galileo turn it to the sky; 1611 Kepler describes the two-convex-lens form; china: 1626 – Schall von Bell's treatise on the telescope; india: c. 1616 – a telescope among Thomas Roe's gifts at Jahangir's court; 1618 Jesuits observe comets by telescope from Goa; east_asia: 1613 – a telescope presented to Tokugawa Ieyasu by the English East India Company
- Read: Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (1610) | Albert Van Helden, The Invention of the Telescope (1977)

## Reflecting telescope `reflecting_telescope`
- Deps: needs telescope; helped by glass_mirrors, copper_bronze
- Core idea: A concave mirror gathers the light instead of a lens, so there are no colour fringes and the instrument can be short and wide. Newton's form: a slightly hollow mirror at the bottom of the tube, a small flat mirror at 45 degrees near the top that throws the image to an eyepiece in the side. The mirror was cast from speculum metal, a white, brittle bronze of roughly two parts copper to one part tin, ground hollow against a convex tool and polished on pitch; it needs repolishing as it tarnishes. For high power the sphere must be deepened to a parabola. From the 1850s a thin layer of silver on glass replaced the metal.
- Pitfalls: Ordinary bronze or a looking-glass mirror will not do (double reflection from glass with a backing) | A mirror surface must be about four times as accurate as a lens surface | Thinking Newton's first instrument outperformed the refractors of its day (it was a proof of principle)
- History: europe: 1616 Zucchi tries; 1663 James Gregory's design; 1668 Newton builds the first working one; 1721 Hadley's parabolic mirror makes it practical; 1789 William Herschel's 1.2 m; 1856–1857 Steinheil and Foucault, silver on glass
- Read: Isaac Newton, An Accompt of a New Catadioptrical Telescope, Philosophical Transactions 7 (1672) | Henry C. King, The History of the Telescope (1955)

## Achromatic lens `achromatic_lens`
- Deps: needs lenses, clear_glass, spectrum_colour
- Core idea: A single lens focuses blue light nearer than red, so images have coloured edges. Two lenses of different glass cemented or mounted together cancel most of this: a convex lens of ordinary (crown) glass with a weaker concave lens of heavy lead (flint) glass, which spreads colours about twice as strongly for the same bending. The pair still focuses, but red and blue now meet. This makes short, sharp telescopes and, later, good microscopes and camera lenses.
- Pitfalls: Using two lenses of the same glass (cannot cancel colour) | Citing Newton, who wrongly concluded it was impossible | Underestimating the glass problem: streak-free flint glass was the bottleneck until Guinand and Fraunhofer
- History: europe: c. 1729–1733 – Chester Moor Hall has the first doublets made; 1758 John Dollond's patent and commercial production; c. 1805–1814 Guinand and Fraunhofer make large homogeneous flint glass; 1830 J. J. Lister's achromatic microscope
- Read: John Dollond, An Account of Some Experiments Concerning the Different Refrangibility of Light, Philosophical Transactions 50 (1758) | Henry C. King, The History of the Telescope (1955)

## Spectrum and the nature of colour `spectrum_colour`
- Deps: helped by refraction_optics, clear_glass
- Core idea: White sunlight is a mixture of all colours. A narrow beam from a hole in the shutter of a dark room, passed through a triangular glass prism, spreads into a band from red to violet because each colour is bent by a different amount. The decisive test: let one colour from the band pass through a second prism; it is bent again but not split or changed. A lens or a reversed prism brings the colours back together to white. The rainbow is the same effect in raindrops: light is refracted, reflected once inside the drop and refracted again, and comes back at about 42 degrees from the point opposite the Sun.
- Pitfalls: Saying the prism adds or creates the colours (the view Newton refuted) | Insisting on exactly seven colours; the band is continuous and Newton's seven follow a musical analogy | Confusing mixing of lights (all give white) with mixing of pigments (give dark brown) | Screen too close to the prism: the band needs several metres to spread
- History: islamic: c. 1300–1309 – Kamal al-Din al-Farisi explains the rainbow with a water-filled glass sphere; europe: c. 1304–1310 – Theodoric of Freiberg, same explanation independently; 1637 Descartes computes the rainbow angle; 1666–1672 Newton's prism experiments; 1704 Opticks; china: 11th c. – Shen Kuo and Sun Sikong ascribe the rainbow to sunlight in raindrops
- Read: Isaac Newton, Opticks (1704) | Carl B. Boyer, The Rainbow: From Myth to Mathematics (1959)

## Spectral analysis `spectroscopy`
- Deps: needs spectrum_colour; helped by telescope, achromatic_lens
- Core idea: Each chemical element, heated in a flame or a spark, gives light of its own fixed colours, which a prism behind a narrow slit shows as sharp bright lines: sodium (common salt) a close yellow doublet, potassium violet, lithium red, copper green. A trace too small to weigh can be identified this way. The Sun's spectrum is crossed by hundreds of dark lines at the same places, because the cooler gas above its surface absorbs those colours; so we can tell what the Sun and stars are made of, and new elements have been found by unknown lines.
- Pitfalls: Without a narrow slit the lines smear into a band | Sodium contamination makes almost every flame yellow | Judging by flame colour alone without the prism
- History: europe: 1752 Melvill notes the yellow line of salt in flames; 1802 Wollaston and 1814 Fraunhofer map dark lines in sunlight; 1859–1861 Kirchhoff and Bunsen establish spectral analysis, discovering caesium in 1860 and rubidium in 1861; 1868 helium seen in the Sun before it is found on Earth (1895)
- Read: Gustav Kirchhoff & Robert Bunsen, Chemische Analyse durch Spectralbeobachtungen, Annalen der Physik 110 (1860) | John B. Hearnshaw, The Analysis of Starlight (1986)

## Waves - sound and light `wave_nature_light_sound`
- Deps: helped by air_pump_vacuum, refraction_optics, spectrum_colour
- Core idea: Sound is a back-and-forth vibration passed on through air (or water, wood, metal) as a wave; nothing travels but the disturbance. It moves about 340 m per second in air, so three seconds between lightning and thunder mean one kilometre. Pitch is the number of vibrations per second; halving a string doubles it and gives the octave. A bell in a jar pumped empty of air falls silent. Light also behaves as a wave, with an extremely short wavelength (about half a thousandth of a millimetre): light from one source passing through two very close slits makes bright and dark stripes, because waves from the two slits add in some places and cancel in others. Colour is wavelength, red longest.
- Pitfalls: Saying sound and light are the same kind of wave: sound needs a medium, light crosses a vacuum | Insisting on a light-carrying ether (assumed until 1905, never detected) | Double-slit demonstration fails with a wide source or slits more than a fraction of a millimetre apart | Claiming light is 'only' a wave; since 1905 it is known to come in quanta as well
- History: greece: 6th c. BC – Pythagorean string ratios (the hammer story is legend); 4th c. BC Aristotle, later Vitruvius, compare sound to ripples; china: c. 3rd c. BC – tuned bells and pitch pipes with numerical rules; 1584 Zhu Zaiyu computes equal temperament; islamic: 10th–11th c. – al-Farabi and Ibn Sina on sound as air in motion; europe: 1636 Mersenne's laws of strings and a measured speed of sound; 1660 Boyle's bell in vacuum; 1665 Grimaldi describes diffraction; 1678–1690 Huygens' wave theory; 1801–1803 Young's interference experiments; 1815–1821 Fresnel; 1865 Maxwell: light is an electromagnetic wave
- Read: Christiaan Huygens, Traité de la lumière (1690) | Thomas Young, Experiments and Calculations Relative to Physical Optics, Philosophical Transactions 94 (1804) | Jed Z. Buchwald, The Rise of the Wave Theory of Light (1989)

## Finite speed of light `speed_of_light`
- Deps: helped by telescope, pendulum_clock, astronomical_distances, heliocentrism
- Core idea: Light is not instantaneous; it travels about 300,000 km per second, so it takes a little over a second from the Moon and about eight minutes from the Sun. First evidence: the eclipses of Jupiter's innermost moon come later than the timetable when the Earth is moving away from Jupiter and earlier when it approaches, in total by about 17 minutes across the Earth's orbit, the time light needs to cross it. On Earth it can be measured with a rapidly spinning toothed wheel or mirror and a mirror several kilometres away.
- Pitfalls: Trying Galileo's lantern test between hills (human reaction time is millions of times too slow) | Saying Rømer measured the speed: he showed it is finite; a value needs the size of the Earth's orbit | Quoting 300,000 km per hour or per minute
- History: greece: 5th c. BC – Empedocles holds that light takes time; Aristotle denies it; islamic: 11th c. – Ibn al-Haytham and al-Biruni argue for a finite speed; europe: 1638 Galileo proposes a lantern test; 1676 Rømer's delay of Io's eclipses (Huygens derives about 220,000 km/s); 1728 Bradley's aberration of starlight; 1849 Fizeau's toothed wheel, 1862 Foucault's rotating mirror (298,000 km/s); americas: 1879–1926 – Michelson's precision measurements
- Read: Ole Rømer, Démonstration touchant le mouvement de la lumière, Journal des Sçavans (1676) | John C. H. Spence, Lightspeed: The Ghostly Aether and the Race to Measure the Speed of Light (2019)

## Photography `photography`
- Deps: helped by camera_obscura, nitric_acid, lenses, achromatic_lens, glassmaking
- Core idea: Some silver salts darken in light. Silver dissolved in nitric acid gives silver nitrate; paper soaked first in weak salt water and then in silver nitrate solution (worked by candlelight) carries silver chloride and turns dark where light falls. Put it in a camera obscura with a lens, or lay a leaf or drawing on it in the sun. The picture must then be fixed, or it blackens all over: wash it in a solution of 'hypo' (sodium thiosulphate), which dissolves the unused silver salt; strong salt water works poorly. Exposure falls from hours to seconds if the invisible latent image is developed chemically (gallic acid on paper, mercury vapour on Daguerre's iodised silver plate). Talbot’s paper negative yields positive contact prints. Each daguerreotype is a unique image on its plate.
- Pitfalls: No fixing step: the image disappears on the first viewing in daylight (Wedgwood's problem in 1802) | Not knowing how to make thiosulphate (boil sulphite solution with sulphur) | Mercury fumes of the daguerreotype process are poisonous; silver nitrate stains and burns skin | Expecting portraits at once: early exposures took minutes to hours
- History: europe: c. 1717–1727 Schulze shows silver salts darken by light, not heat; 1802 Wedgwood and Davy, unfixed images; 1826 or 1827 Niépce's first surviving camera picture (bitumen); 1839 Daguerre and Talbot announce their processes, Herschel introduces hypo; 1841 calotype; 1851 Archer's wet collodion; 1871 Maddox's gelatine dry plate; americas: 1888 – Eastman's roll-film Kodak
- Read: William Henry Fox Talbot, The Pencil of Nature (1844) | Helmut Gernsheim with Alison Gernsheim, The History of Photography from the Earliest Use of the Camera Obscura in the Eleventh Century up to 1914 (1955)

## Lever, pulley, inclined plane (statics) `lever_mechanics_statics`
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof
- Core idea: A lever balances when weight times distance from the pivot is equal on both sides; an effort arm ten times the load arm can lift the load with a tenth of its weight in applied force. The same rule governs every simple machine: what is gained in force is lost in distance moved. A tackle with four rope strands holding the lower block lifts with a quarter of the force but four times the rope; a ramp four times as long as it is high needs a quarter of the weight to push a load up it (friction apart); a screw is a ramp wound round a cylinder. With this rule a builder can calculate cranes, presses and steelyards before making them.
- Pitfalls: Promising a machine that multiplies both force and distance (perpetual motion) | Ignoring friction and rope stiffness, which eat a third or more in real tackles | Measuring lever arms along the beam rather than at right angles to the force | Assuming Archimedes invented the lever; he proved its law
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2300–2000 BC – shaduf (counterweighted lever) shown on Akkadian seals; egypt: c. 2600 BC – levers, ramps and sledges in pyramid building; equal-arm balance earlier still; china: c. 4th–3rd c. BC – Mohist Canon discusses lever and balance; steelyard in use; greece: c. 4th–3rd c. BC Aristotelian Mechanical Problems; c. 250 BC Archimedes proves the law of the lever; compound pulley attributed to him; 1st c. AD Hero lists the five simple machines; islamic: 9th c. – Thabit ibn Qurra on the steelyard; 1121 al-Khazini, Balance of Wisdom; europe: 13th c. Jordanus; 1586 Stevin solves the inclined plane; c. 1600 Galileo, On Mechanics
- Read: Archimedes, On the Equilibrium of Planes (c. 250 BC) | E. J. Dijksterhuis, Archimedes (1956)

## Buoyancy and hydrostatics `buoyancy_hydrostatics`
- Deps: helped by lever_mechanics_statics
- Core idea: A body in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. So it floats if it is lighter than the same volume of water, and an iron ship floats if its hull encloses enough air. Weighing an object in air and again hanging in water gives its density and so detects alloyed gold: gold is 19.3 times as heavy as water, silver 10.5, lead 11.3, copper 8.9. Pressure in a liquid depends only on depth, not on the shape or width of the vessel (about one atmosphere per 10 m of water), and pressure applied to an enclosed liquid acts equally everywhere, which is the principle of the hydraulic press.
- Pitfalls: Telling the crown story with the overflowing bath; the overflow is too small to measure, the practical method is the balance in water | Believing heavy things sink because they are heavy rather than dense | Thinking a wider water column presses harder at the bottom | Confusing displaced mass with volume: at the same load, a floating ship displaces the same mass but a smaller volume in salt water
- History: greece: c. 250 BC – Archimedes, On Floating Bodies; china: c. 200 AD – story of Cao Chong weighing an elephant by the sinking of a boat (Sanguozhi); islamic: 11th c. al-Biruni and 1121 al-Khazini measure specific gravities of metals and gems to about 1 per cent; europe: 1586 Galileo's little balance; 1586 Stevin's hydrostatic paradox; 1653 Pascal's treatise (published 1663); 1795 Bramah's hydraulic press
- Read: Archimedes, On Floating Bodies (c. 250 BC) | Vitruvius, De architectura IX, preface | E. J. Dijksterhuis, Archimedes (1956)

## Falling bodies and projectiles `falling_bodies`
- Deps: helped by mechanical_clock, symbolic_algebra
- Core idea: Apart from air resistance, all bodies fall at the same rate whatever their weight: a heavy and a light ball dropped together from a tower land together. The speed grows steadily (about 10 m/s more every second) and the distance grows with the square of the time: about 5 m in the first second, 20 m after two, 45 m after three. It can be shown slowly by rolling a ball down a grooved ramp and marking positions at equal beats: the gaps go as 1, 3, 5, 7. A thrown or fired body keeps its forward motion while it falls, so its path is a parabola, and the longest range on level ground is near 45 degrees, less for fast shot in air.
- Pitfalls: Dropping a feather or paper to 'prove' it and being refuted by air resistance; use two dense balls | Citing the Leaning Tower experiment as fact (it rests only on Viviani's late account) | Saying speed is proportional to distance fallen (Galileo's own first error); it is proportional to time | Applying the vacuum parabola to cannon shot, which falls far short
- History: greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotle: heavier bodies fall faster in proportion to weight; egypt: c. 530 AD – John Philoponus (Byzantine Alexandria) reports that unequal weights fall in nearly equal times; islamic: 12th c. – Abu'l-Barakat al-Baghdadi describes acceleration of fall as accumulating impetus; europe: 14th c. Merton scholars and Oresme, mean-speed theorem; 1537 Tartaglia on gunnery; 1551 de Soto calls fall uniformly accelerated; 1586 Stevin's drop test at Delft; c. 1604–1609 Galileo's ramp experiments, published 1638
- Read: Galileo Galilei, Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze (1638) | Stillman Drake, Galileo at Work: His Scientific Biography (1978)

## Laws of motion `laws_of_motion`
- Deps: helped by falling_bodies, symbolic_algebra, calculus
- Core idea: First: a body left alone keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed; it does not need a push to keep going, and things on Earth stop only because of friction and air. Second: a force changes the motion, and the change of velocity per second equals the force divided by the mass (F = m a). Third: forces come in pairs; whatever pushes is pushed back equally (a gun recoils, a rower pushes water backwards). Uniform motion in a straight line cannot be felt, which is why we do not notice the moving Earth: a stone dropped from the mast of a smoothly sailing ship lands at the foot of the mast.
- Pitfalls: Accepting the common-sense Aristotelian view that motion needs a continuing force | Confusing mass with weight, or force with energy or momentum | Stating inertia as circular motion (Galileo's own version) | Inventing a 'centrifugal force' that throws things outward; they simply go straight on
- History: china: c. 4th–3rd c. BC – a Mohist Canon passage says motion stops only through an opposing force (reading disputed); egypt: c. 530 AD – Philoponus (Byzantine Alexandria) proposes an impressed force against Aristotle; islamic: 11th c. Ibn Sina: impressed 'mayl' would persist in a void; 12th c. Ibn Bajja and al-Baghdadi; europe: c. 1350 Buridan's impetus; 1632–1638 Galileo; 1644 Descartes states straight-line inertia; 1687 Newton's three laws
- Read: Isaac Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687) | I. Bernard Cohen, The Birth of a New Physics (1960)

## Universal gravitation `universal_gravitation`
- Deps: needs laws_of_motion, keplers_laws; helped by calculus, falling_bodies, astronomical_distances
- Core idea: Every body attracts every other with a force proportional to both masses and falling off with the square of the distance. The force that makes an apple fall is the same that holds the Moon: the Moon is 60 Earth radii away, so it should fall towards the Earth 3600 times more slowly than the apple, about 1.4 mm in a second instead of 4.9 m, and that is exactly how much its path curves away from a straight line. The same law gives Kepler's three laws, the tides, the flattening of the Earth at the poles and the return of comets. A planet is a projectile that keeps falling round the Sun without reaching it.
- Pitfalls: Saying Newton 'discovered gravity' or that the apple hit his head; his step was that the force reaches the Moon and follows one law | Thinking there is no gravity in orbit; orbiting is continuous falling | Leaving out the inverse square, without which nothing can be calculated | Being unable to answer 'what is the cause of the attraction?' (Newton declined to say; that is acceptable)
- History: india: 628 – Brahmagupta writes that the Earth attracts bodies as water flows; a qualitative remark, not a law; europe: 1609 Kepler suggests a solar force; 1645 Boulliau mentions an inverse square; 1679–1680 Hooke proposes it to Newton; 1687 Newton, Principia; 1736–1737 Lapland expedition confirms the flattened Earth; 1759 return of Halley's comet; 1798 Cavendish weighs the Earth; 1846 Neptune found by calculation
- Read: Isaac Newton, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687) | Richard S. Westfall, Never at Rest: A Biography of Isaac Newton (1980)

## Strength of materials and scaling `strength_of_materials`
- Deps: helped by lever_mechanics_statics, symbolic_algebra
- Core idea: Within the proportional range, a material stretches in proportion to the load (Hooke's law), and each has a breaking stress, a load per unit of cross-section, that can be measured by hanging weights on a wire or rod. A rope or tie twice as thick carries four times the load. A beam's stiffness and strength grow far more with depth than with width, so a plank on edge carries much more than flat. A slender column fails by buckling sideways long before it is crushed, and doubling its length quarters the load it bears. Because weight grows with the cube of size and strength only with the square, a model that stands does not prove the full-size structure will.
- Pitfalls: Scaling up a working model in all dimensions and expecting it to hold | Trusting stone, brick or cast iron in tension or bending (strong only in compression) | No safety factor for flaws, knots and shock loads | Confusing stiffness with strength
- History: europe: c. 1490s Leonardo's notes on testing wires and beams; 1638 Galileo on beams and the square-cube law; 1678 Hooke's law; 1744–1757 Euler's buckling formula; 1773 Coulomb; 1826 Navier's theory of bending; china: 1103 – Yingzao fashi fixes proportional sizes for timber members (rules of practice, not theory)
- Read: Galileo Galilei, Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze (1638) | Stephen P. Timoshenko, History of Strength of Materials (1953) | J. E. Gordon, Structures: Or Why Things Don't Fall Down (1978)

## Sundial and water clock `sundial_water_clock`
- Deps: helped by round_earth_size, geometry_proof
- Core idea: A sundial tells the time from the direction of a shadow. On a simple dial for equal hours the shadow-casting edge points at the celestial pole, that is, slopes towards the visible pole at an angle equal to the absolute latitude. Each dial is correct only for the latitude it was made for, and it shows local solar time, which varies from local mean solar time by up to about 16 minutes. A water clock measures time by water running through a small hole. Flow slows as the level falls. Calibrate unequal level marks on an outflow clock, or supply an inflow clock from a constant-level tank. The smallest readable interval depends on the scale and the steadiness of the flow or shadow.
- Pitfalls: Vertical gnomon with equally spaced hour marks | Carrying a dial to another latitude (Rome used a looted Sicilian dial wrongly for about 99 years, according to Pliny) | Treating Greek or Roman seasonal hours as fixed lengths: daylight and darkness were each divided into twelve | Marking equal intervals on a straight-sided outflow vessel as if the flow stayed constant, or ignoring changes of flow in the cold
- History: egypt: c. 1500 BC shadow clocks; c. 1400 BC outflow water clock (Karnak, reign of Amenhotep III); mesopotamia: 2nd millennium BC – water clocks measured by weight of water; gnomon in use by c. 700 BC; china: gnomon observations from the 2nd millennium BC; inflow water clocks with compensating tanks by the Han; greece: 6th c. BC gnomon from Babylon (Herodotus); c. 270 BC Ctesibius' regulated water clock; c. 50 BC Tower of the Winds, Athens; rome: Pliny reports a tradition of a sundial dedicated by Papirius Cursor in 293 BC. Varro dates the first public dial near the Rostra to 263 BC, brought from Catina in Sicily. Scipio Nasica installed a public water clock during his censorship in 159 BC.; islamic: 1371 – Ibn al-Shatir's dial in Damascus with pole-pointing gnomon and equal hours; europe: 15th c. – pole-pointing dials become standard
- Read: Pliny the Elder, Natural History VII.213–215 | Vitruvius, De architectura IX.7–8 | Gerhard Dohrn-van Rossum, History of the Hour: Clocks and Modern Temporal Orders (1996)

## Mechanical clock (escapement, spring drive) `mechanical_clock`
- Deps: needs gears_gear_trains; helped by wire_drawing, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: A falling weight on a cord turns a train of gears; an escapement lets the train advance only one tooth at a time, so the weight runs down in steps instead of crashing. In the verge escapement a crown wheel with saw teeth pushes two small plates (pallets) on an upright rod alternately; the rod carries a crossbar with movable weights (foliot) or a wheel (balance) that swings to and fro and sets the rate. Such clocks err by a quarter of an hour a day or more and are set by a sundial. A coiled steel spring instead of the weight makes the clock portable; a cone-shaped fusee evens out the spring's weakening pull. Real accuracy comes only with the pendulum (1656) and the balance spring (1675).
- Pitfalls: Describing gears and hands but no escapement; that is the whole invention | Jumping straight to a pendulum or a watch without the metalworking (hardened steel springs, cut pinions) | Promising minute accuracy from a verge and foliot | Calling Henlein the inventor of the watch (small spring clocks existed before him)
- History: china: 725 Yi Xing and Liang Lingzan's water-driven armillary with a stop-release linkage; 1088–1094 Su Song's astronomical clock tower, Kaifeng; islamic: 11th c. al-Muradi's geared water clocks; 1206 al-Jazari's automata clocks; c. 1560 Taqi al-Din describes weight and spring clocks; europe: c. 1270–1300 weight-driven verge clock (Dunstable 1283 is the first likely record); 1364 de Dondi's Astrarium; c. 1430 spring drive and fusee; c. 1500–1510 portable watches in Nuremberg and Italy; 1675 balance spring (Huygens; Hooke claims priority)
- Read: David S. Landes, Revolution in Time (1983) | Joseph Needham, Wang Ling & Derek J. de Solla Price, Heavenly Clockwork (1960) | Carlo M. Cipolla, Clocks and Culture 1300–1700 (1967)

## Pendulum clock `pendulum_clock`
- Deps: needs mechanical_clock; helped by falling_bodies
- Core idea: A weight swinging on a rod or thread takes the same time for every swing as long as the swings are small; the time depends only on the length, not on the weight, and goes with the square root of the length. A pendulum about 99.4 cm long beats seconds (one second each way); a quarter of that length beats half seconds. Let the pendulum, not a foliot, control the escapement, which in turn gives it a small push each swing: the error falls from a quarter of an hour a day to under a minute, with a long pendulum and anchor escapement to a few seconds. A bare pendulum counted by hand already times experiments and pulses.
- Pitfalls: Wide swings (period then depends on the arc); keep them to a few degrees | Thinking a heavier bob swings faster | Ignoring heat: a metal rod lengthens in summer and the clock loses | Expecting it to work at sea; a rolling ship ruins it | Repeating the myth that Ibn Yunus used a pendulum for timekeeping around 1000
- History: europe: 1602 Galileo's first letter on the pendulum's equal swings (the cathedral-lamp story of 1583 comes from Viviani); 1637–1641 Galileo's clock design; 1656 Huygens' design, built 1657 by Salomon Coster; c. 1657–1671 anchor escapement (Clement or Hooke); 1721 Graham's mercury compensation, 1726 Harrison's gridiron; china: 17th c. – brought by Jesuits to the Qing court
- Read: Christiaan Huygens, Horologium Oscillatorium (1673) | David S. Landes, Revolution in Time (1983)

## Air pressure and the barometer `atmospheric_pressure`
- Deps: helped by glassmaking, mercury_amalgam, buoyancy_hydrostatics
- Core idea: Air has weight, and we live at the bottom of an ocean of it that presses on everything with about 1 kg on every square centimetre. That, not 'nature's horror of a vacuum', is why a suction pump lifts water: the air pushes it up, and only to about 10 m. Fill a glass tube a metre long, closed at one end, with mercury, and upend it in a bowl of mercury: the column sinks to about 76 cm and leaves empty space above. Carried up a mountain the column falls (about 1 cm per 100 m), and it changes with the weather.
- Pitfalls: Saying a vacuum sucks; nothing pulls, the outside air pushes | Confusing air pressure with steam pressure | Air bubbles or damp left in the tube spoil the column | Mercury vapour is poisonous; do not heat or spill it indoors | Trying the experiment with water without a 10.5 m tube
- History: greece: 3rd c. BC – Strato argues for empty spaces between particles and Ctesibius uses compressed air. Hero discusses air and void in his Pneumatica in the 1st c. AD; islamic: 1121 – al-Khazini treats air as having weight and buoyancy and as thinning with height; europe: c. 1630 Baliani and Beeckman ascribe the pump limit to the weight of air; c. 1641 Berti's water column in Rome; 1643–1644 Torricelli and Viviani's mercury tube; 1648 Périer's ascent of the Puy de Dôme for Pascal; 1654–1657 Guericke's hemispheres
- Read: Blaise Pascal, Traités de l'équilibre des liqueurs et de la pesanteur de la masse de l'air (1663) | W. E. Knowles Middleton, The History of the Barometer (1964)

## Air pump and vacuum experiments `air_pump_vacuum`
- Deps: needs piston_pump; helped by atmospheric_pressure, boring_machine, glassmaking
- Core idea: A piston pump with two valves, turned round so that it draws air out of a closed vessel instead of water out of a well. Each stroke removes a fraction of what is left. Everything depends on tightness: a truly round barrel, a leather piston soaked in oil, joints sealed with wax or kept under water, a tap between pump and vessel. In the emptied glass a candle goes out, a bell can hardly be heard, warm water boils, and a feather falls as fast as a coin. Two close-fitting copper bowls emptied of air cannot be pulled apart by teams of horses. Much later the same art gives light bulbs and electron tubes.
- Pitfalls: Expecting a perfect vacuum; early pumps reached perhaps a tenth to a hundredth of an atmosphere | Thin or flat-sided glass vessels implode; use thick round ones | Leaks at every joint; without constant sealing nothing works, as Boyle's critics found
- History: europe: c. 1647–1650 Guericke's first pump; 1654 Regensburg and 1657 Magdeburg hemisphere shows; 1659 Boyle and Hooke's pump with glass receiver; 1705 Hauksbee's double-barrel pump; 1855 Geissler and 1865 Sprengel mercury pumps; china: double-acting piston bellows long in use, but no evacuation pump before European contact
- Read: Robert Boyle, New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, Touching the Spring of the Air (1660) | Steven Shapin & Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985)

## Thermometer and temperature scale `thermometer_temperature`
- Deps: needs glassmaking; helped by distillation, mercury_amalgam, atmospheric_pressure
- Core idea: In a sealed liquid thermometer, expansion of the liquid in a bulb moves a column along a narrow tube of uniform bore. For a mercury Celsius thermometer, mark melting ice and steam above boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure, then divide the interval into 100 equal parts. Compare a spirit thermometer with a calibrated instrument over its working range. Readings can now be compared in medicine, brewing and weather records. A cup and a tub can have the same temperature although warming the tub by one degree takes more energy.
- Pitfalls: An open tube standing in water (the early thermoscope) also responds to air pressure | Boiling point falls with altitude and with a low barometer (about 1 degree per 300 m) | Ethanol boils near 78 °C at atmospheric pressure. A boiling-water calibration is unsuitable for an ordinary spirit thermometer | Uneven bore gives unequal degrees | Scale by guesswork ('hottest summer day') instead of reproducible fixed points
- History: greece: 3rd c. BC Philo of Byzantium and 1st c. AD Hero show air expanding with heat; europe: c. 1593–1603 Galileo's circle, air thermoscope; 1612 Santorio adds a scale and uses it on patients; c. 1654 sealed spirit thermometers of Grand Duke Ferdinando II, Florence; 1714 Fahrenheit's mercury thermometer; 1742 Celsius' centigrade scale (first with 100 at freezing; reversed within a few years); 1848 Kelvin's absolute scale
- Read: W. E. Knowles Middleton, A History of the Thermometer and Its Use in Meteorology (1966) | Hasok Chang, Inventing Temperature: Measurement and Scientific Progress (2004)

## Specific and latent heat `latent_specific_heat`
- Deps: needs thermometer_temperature
- Core idea: Different substances need different amounts of heat for the same rise in temperature; water has a high specific heat (about ten times as much as iron, weight for weight). Melting and boiling swallow large amounts of heat with no rise in temperature at all: melting ice takes as much heat as warming the same water from 0 to 80 degrees, and turning boiling water into steam takes more than five times what was needed to bring it from freezing to the boil. That is why ice lasts, why steam scalds worse than boiling water, and why an engine that cools and reheats its cylinder at every stroke wastes most of its fuel.
- Pitfalls: Assuming ice at 0 degrees turns to water as soon as it reaches 0 | Treating heat and temperature as the same thing | Expecting water to get hotter the harder it is boiled
- History: europe: c. 1757–1762 Joseph Black (Glasgow) establishes latent and specific heat in lectures; 1764–1765 Watt applies it to the steam engine; 1772 Wilcke publishes independently; 1780s Lavoisier and Laplace's ice calorimeter
- Read: Joseph Black, Lectures on the Elements of Chemistry (1803) | D. S. L. Cardwell, From Watt to Clausius (1971)

## Heat as motion, conservation of energy, limits of engines `heat_energy_conservation`
- Deps: needs thermometer_temperature; helped by latent_specific_heat, laws_of_motion, atomic_theory, gas_laws
- Core idea: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Internal energy includes the microscopic motion and interactions of the particles of matter. Work can be turned into heat without limit (boring a cannon with a blunt tool boils water for as long as the horses turn), and always at the same rate: the work of letting 1 kg fall about 427 m warms 1 kg of water by one degree. Energy in all its forms (motion, height, heat, chemical, electrical) is never created or destroyed, only converted, so no machine can give out more work than it takes in. The other way is limited: an engine turns heat into work only while heat flows from hot to cold, and the largest possible share is the temperature drop divided by the hot temperature counted from absolute zero (-273 degrees C). Hotter steam and a colder condenser mean less fuel.
- Pitfalls: Proposing or funding perpetual motion machines | Describing heat as a substance (caloric) that flows out of bodies | Saying energy is 'used up'; it is degraded to lukewarm heat | Expecting an engine to convert all the heat of its fuel into work
- History: europe: 1620 Bacon and 1738 Daniel Bernoulli: heat is motion; 1798 Rumford's cannon-boring experiment; 1824 Carnot on the motive power of fire; 1842 Mayer; 1843–1850 Joule measures the mechanical equivalent; 1847 Helmholtz states conservation generally; 1850–1865 Clausius and Kelvin, second law and entropy; 1860s–1870s Maxwell and Boltzmann, kinetic theory
- Read: Sadi Carnot, Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu (1824) | James Prescott Joule, On the Mechanical Equivalent of Heat, Philosophical Transactions 140 (1850) | D. S. L. Cardwell, From Watt to Clausius (1971)

## Weather instruments and forecasting `weather_instruments`
- Deps: helped by atmospheric_pressure, thermometer_temperature, electric_telegraph, data_graphs
- Core idea: Weather can be measured and, a day or so ahead, foretold. A falling barometer warns of wind and rain, a fast fall of a storm; a rising one of fair weather. Storms are huge whirling systems hundreds of kilometres across that travel, in the middle latitudes mostly from west to east, so that yesterday's weather upwind is tomorrow's here. In the northern hemisphere, with the wind at your back, the low pressure lies to your left. Useful instruments: barometer, thermometer, a rain gauge (a straight-sided vessel, depth read with a ruler), a wind vane, and a hygrometer (a degreased hair or gut string that lengthens in damp air). Daily readings at fixed hours at many places, collected on one map, show the systems moving.
- Pitfalls: Reading the barometer's level instead of its change | Promising forecasts weeks ahead or for an exact place and hour | Readings in the sun or at irregular times cannot be compared | Explaining weather by the Moon's phases or the planets
- History: india: c. 3rd c. BC–2nd c. AD – Arthashastra prescribes rain measurement in a standard bowl; china: c. 120 BC Huainanzi: charcoal on a balance shows humidity; wind vanes in use under the Han; 1247 Qin Jiushao on rain and snow gauges; east_asia: 1441–1442 – Korea: standard rain gauge (cheugugi) under Sejong, credited to the crown prince, issued to all provinces; greece: c. 340 BC Aristotle, Meteorologica; c. 50 BC wind vane on the Tower of the Winds; europe: c. 1450 Cusanus and Alberti describe hygrometer and anemometer; 1654 Medici network of observers; 1660 Guericke foretells a storm from the barometer; 1783 Saussure's hair hygrometer; 1820 Brandes' first weather maps; 1857 Buys Ballot's law; 1861 FitzRoy's telegraph-based storm warnings and forecasts; 1919 Bergen school, fronts; americas: 1743 – Franklin notes that storms travel against their own surface wind
- Read: W. E. Knowles Middleton, Invention of the Meteorological Instruments (1969) | Peter Moore, The Weather Experiment (2015)

## Spherical Earth and its size `round_earth_size`
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, sundial_water_clock
- Core idea: The Earth is a ball about 40,000 km round (a degree of latitude is about 111 km). Evidence anyone can check: a ship's hull disappears below the horizon before its mast; the Earth's shadow on the Moon in a lunar eclipse is always round; travelling south, new stars rise and the Pole Star sinks; the same eclipse is seen at a later hour of the night further east. Its size: at noon on midsummer day the Sun stood overhead at Syene but 7.2 degrees (a fiftieth of a circle) from overhead at Alexandria, 5000 stadia north, so the whole circle is 50 times that distance. People on the other side do not fall off because 'down' everywhere means towards the centre.
- Pitfalls: Telling educated people of ancient Greece, Rome, the Islamic world or medieval Europe that they believe in a flat Earth; they do not | Saying Columbus proved the Earth round; the dispute was its size, and he was wrong (he made it a quarter too small and Asia too wide) | Claiming Eratosthenes was exact to 1 per cent; the length of his stadion is uncertain | Forgetting that the method assumes the Sun's rays are parallel and the two places lie north-south
- History: greece: 5th c. BC Pythagoreans and Parmenides; c. 350 BC Aristotle's proofs; c. 240 BC Eratosthenes measures 250,000–252,000 stadia; india: 499 – Aryabhata: a rotating sphere, with a circumference close to the true one; islamic: c. 830 al-Ma'mun's surveyors measure a degree in the Sinjar plain; c. 1020s al-Biruni's mountain-and-horizon method near Nandana; china: a flat Earth under a round heaven remained usual until Jesuit teaching in the 17th c., despite Zhang Heng's 'egg yolk' image (c. 120 AD); mesopotamia: flat disc surrounded by ocean (Babylonian world map, c. 6th c. BC); europe: known throughout the Middle Ages (Bede 725; Sacrobosco, De sphaera, c. 1230); 1519–1522 Magellan and Elcano's circumnavigation; 1669–1670 Picard's accurate degree
- Read: Aristotle, On the Heavens II.14 | Cleomedes, On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies (account of Eratosthenes' measurement) | Jeffrey Burton Russell, Inventing the Flat Earth: Columbus and Modern Historians (1991)

## Cause of the seasons (tilted axis) `seasons_axial_tilt`
- Deps: needs round_earth_size; helped by heliocentrism, sundial_water_clock
- Core idea: The seasons come from the tilt of the Earth's axis, about 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular to its orbital plane (in the older picture: the Sun's yearly path is inclined by that much to the celestial equator). In summer the Sun stands higher, its rays strike more steeply and the day is longer; in winter the reverse. Therefore the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres, the Sun passes overhead only between the tropics, and beyond about 66.5 degrees latitude there are days when it does not set. The tilt is measured from the noon shadow of a vertical pole at the two solstices: outside the tropics, where the Sun is above the horizon at both noons, half the difference between the two Sun heights.
- Pitfalls: Saying summer comes because the Earth is nearer the Sun; it is nearest in early January | Forgetting that the southern hemisphere has the opposite season | Saying the axis wobbles to and fro during the year; it keeps its direction
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1000 BC – MUL.APIN lists solstices, equinoxes and changing day length; china: gnomon shadow measurements of the solstices from the 1st millennium BC (Zhoubi suanjing); greece: 5th c. BC Oenopides credited with the obliquity; c. 240 BC Eratosthenes measures it as about 23 degrees 51 minutes; india: 499 – Aryabhata gives 24 degrees; islamic: 9th–10th c. – repeated measurements show the obliquity slowly decreasing; americas: solstice and zenith-passage alignments in Mesoamerican and Andean sites
- Read: James Evans, The History and Practice of Ancient Astronomy (1998) | Otto Neugebauer, The Exact Sciences in Antiquity (1957)

## Cause and prediction of eclipses `eclipse_prediction`
- Deps: helped by round_earth_size, arabic_numerals, solar_calendar_leap_years
- Core idea: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight. A lunar eclipse happens at full moon when the Moon passes through the Earth's shadow; a solar eclipse at new moon when the Moon covers the Sun. They do not happen every month because the Moon's path is tilted about 5 degrees to the Sun's, so the three line up only near the two crossing points. Eclipses repeat in a cycle of 223 lunar months, which is 18 years and 11 days plus about 8 hours (the saros): from a list of past eclipses, the next ones can be foretold. A lunar eclipse is seen from the whole night side of the Earth, a total solar eclipse only along a narrow track, so lunar ones are the safe prediction.
- Pitfalls: Ignoring the extra 8 hours: the next eclipse of a series falls a third of the globe further west, so it may not be visible locally | Predicting a solar eclipse for a given town from the cycle alone | Looking at a partial solar eclipse with bare eyes (blinds) | Citing Thales' prediction of 585 BC as certain; it is doubted | A stranded traveller rarely remembers actual dates; without an almanac or records the 'Columbus trick' cannot be done
- History: mesopotamia: eclipse records from c. 750 BC; saros-based prediction of lunar eclipses by c. 600 BC, later arithmetic theories; china: oracle-bone eclipse records c. 1200 BC; 1st c. BC–2nd c. AD Jing Fang and Zhang Heng give the shadow explanation; 3rd c. AD calendars predict lunar eclipses; solar predictions stay unreliable until the 17th c.; greece: c. 450 BC Anaxagoras explains both kinds; c. 140 BC Hipparchus; c. 100 BC Antikythera mechanism with saros dial; c. 150 AD Ptolemy, Almagest; india: 499 – Aryabhata computes eclipses from shadows, against the Rahu myth; islamic: 9th–10th c. – al-Khwarizmi's and al-Battani's tables; americas: Maya eclipse-warning table in the Dresden Codex (copy of c. 1200, older sources); europe: 1474 Regiomontanus' printed Ephemerides (used by Columbus in Jamaica, 1504); 1715 Halley's map of a solar eclipse track
- Read: Otto Neugebauer, The Exact Sciences in Antiquity (1957) | John M. Steele, Observations and Predictions of Eclipse Times by Early Astronomers (2000) | F. Richard Stephenson, Historical Eclipses and Earth's Rotation (1997)

## Heliocentric model `heliocentrism`
- Deps: needs round_earth_size; helped by telescope, laws_of_motion, keplers_laws
- Core idea: The Earth turns on its axis once a day and travels round the Sun once a year, as the third of the planets; only the Moon goes round the Earth. This explains at one stroke why the planets sometimes move backwards (the Earth overtakes them), why Mercury and Venus never stray far from the Sun, and the order and relative distances of the planets. Evidence with a small telescope: Venus shows a full set of phases like the Moon and changes size, so it circles the Sun; Jupiter has four moons, so not everything circles the Earth. We do not feel the motion because everything on Earth shares it.
- Pitfalls: Claiming Copernicus's system predicted better or was simpler; with circles it still needed epicycles and was no more accurate than Ptolemy | Having no answer to the serious objections: no visible shift of the stars through the year (they are immensely far) and no wind or falling behind (inertia) | Presenting the phases of Venus as proof; they refute Ptolemy but also fit Tycho's system, in which the planets circle a Sun that circles the Earth | Saying the Sun is the fixed centre of the universe | Underestimating the religious and legal risk after 1616, or inventing it before
- History: greece: c. 270 BC Aristarchus of Samos; c. 150 BC Seleucus of Seleucia defends it; rejected by Hipparchus and Ptolemy; india: 499 – Aryabhata teaches the daily rotation of the Earth (his planetary model stays geocentric); islamic: 13th–14th c. al-Tusi and Ibn al-Shatir devise the geometrical tools Copernicus later uses, in geocentric models; Earth's rotation debated by al-Biruni and at Maragha; europe: 1543 Copernicus, De revolutionibus; 1609–1619 Kepler; 1610 Galileo's telescope observations; 1616 Copernicus's book suspended, 1633 Galileo's trial; 1728 Bradley's aberration, first direct proof of the Earth's motion; 1838 Bessel's stellar parallax; 1851 Foucault's pendulum shows the rotation
- Read: Nicolaus Copernicus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543) | Galileo Galilei, Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo (1632) | Thomas S. Kuhn, The Copernican Revolution (1957)

## Kepler's laws of planetary motion `keplers_laws`
- Deps: needs heliocentrism; helped by geometry_proof, logarithms, coordinate_geometry
- Core idea: First, each planet moves in an ellipse (a slightly flattened circle, drawn with a loop of thread round two pins) with the Sun at one of the two pin points, not at the centre. Second, it moves faster when nearer the Sun, such that the line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. Third, the square of the time of revolution is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis: with years and the Earth's distance as units, Jupiter at 5.2 takes 11.86 years. Kepler used these laws and Tycho’s observations to predict the date of the 1631 Mercury transit. Gassendi observed it about five hours earlier than predicted.
- Pitfalls: Drawing strongly elongated orbits; planetary ellipses are almost circles, the Sun being off-centre is the noticeable part | Putting the Sun at the centre of the ellipse | Explaining the seasons by the changing distance | Offering the laws without data; they were won from Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars and convince only by better predictions
- History: europe: 1609 Astronomia nova (first two laws, from Tycho's Mars data); 1619 Harmonices mundi (third law); 1627 Rudolphine Tables; 1631 Gassendi sees the predicted transit of Mercury; 1687 Newton derives the laws from gravitation; islamic: 11th c. – al-Zarqali uses an oval deferent for Mercury (a geometrical device, not an orbit law)
- Read: Johannes Kepler, Astronomia nova (1609) and Tabulae Rudolphinae (1627) | James R. Voelkel, Johannes Kepler and the New Astronomy (1999)

## Distances of Moon, Sun and stars (parallax) `astronomical_distances`
- Deps: needs round_earth_size, trigonometry; helped by telescope, keplers_laws, pendulum_clock
- Core idea: Distances in the sky are found like a surveyor's: observe the same body from two places a known distance apart and measure how far it shifts against the background (parallax). The Moon is about 60 Earth radii away (384,000 km), found already in antiquity. The Sun is about 150 million km away, some 400 times further than the Moon and 109 Earth diameters wide; this needed telescopes and observers on different continents (Mars in 1672, Venus crossing the Sun in 1761 and 1769). Kepler's third law then gives all other planets. The nearest stars are a few hundred thousand times further than the Sun; their yearly shift as the Earth moves is under one second of arc and was first measured in 1838.
- Pitfalls: Quoting the modern figures without any method; the numbers alone convince nobody | Using Aristarchus' half-moon method, which is sound geometry but gave a Sun 20 times too near | Expecting to see stellar parallax with early instruments; its absence was the main argument against Copernicus
- History: greece: c. 270 BC Aristarchus: Sun about 19 times further than the Moon; c. 140 BC Hipparchus: Moon at about 60 Earth radii; Ptolemy's solar distance of about 1200 Earth radii stays standard for 1500 years; islamic: 9th–11th c. – al-Farghani and al-Battani refine the Ptolemaic distances; europe: 1672 Cassini and Richer, parallax of Mars: Sun about 140 million km; 1761 and 1769 transits of Venus observed worldwide; 1838 Bessel, parallax of 61 Cygni; americas: 1912 – Henrietta Leavitt's period-luminosity law for variable stars opens distances beyond parallax
- Read: Albert Van Helden, Measuring the Universe: Cosmic Dimensions from Aristarchus to Halley (1985) | Alan W. Hirshfeld, Parallax: The Race to Measure the Cosmos (2001)

## Comets as orbiting bodies `comets_orbits`
- Deps: helped by universal_gravitation, keplers_laws, telescope
- Core idea: Comets are not vapours in the air or omens but bodies far beyond the Moon that travel round the Sun on paths that are often very elongated. Bound comets can return. Proof of the distance: observers hundreds of kilometres apart see a comet at the same place among the stars, whereas the Moon shifts noticeably. The solar wind drives the ion tail away from the Sun. Dust pushed by sunlight also retains orbital motion and forms a curved tail. The bright comet seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 is one body with a period of about 76 years.
- Pitfalls: Predicting a return from memory with a wrong year, or assuming every comet is periodic on human timescales | Saying the tail trails behind the motion | Dismissing the fear of comets without offering the parallax argument
- History: china: systematic comet records from 613 BC; Halley's comet recorded in 240 BC; the Book of Jin (compiled c. AD 648, astronomical treatise, ch. 12) describes tails pointing east in the evening and west in the morning; mesopotamia: 164 BC – Babylonian diaries record Halley's comet; rome: c. 65 AD – Seneca argues that comets are lasting bodies on orbits (Natural Questions VII); europe: 1531–1540 Apian and Fracastoro: tails point away from the Sun; 1577 Tycho Brahe shows a comet is beyond the Moon; 1705 Halley predicts a return, confirmed in 1758–1759
- Read: Book of Jin (Jin shu), ch. 12, astronomical treatise (7th c. AD) | Edmond Halley, A Synopsis of the Astronomy of Comets (1705) | Donald K. Yeomans, Comets: A Chronological History of Observation, Science, Myth, and Folklore (1991)

## Tides caused by Moon and Sun `tides`
- Deps: helped by universal_gravitation, eclipse_prediction
- Core idea: The tides follow the Moon. At many ports high water comes twice in about 24 hours 50 minutes, so each day roughly 50 minutes later, like the Moon's rising. The range is greatest just after new and full moon (spring tides), when Sun and Moon pull along the same line, and smallest at the half moons (neap tides). At a given harbour, high water follows the Moon's passage across the meridian by a characteristic average interval, which can be found by a month of observation and then used for a tide table. The cause is the Moon's attraction being stronger on the near side of the Earth and weaker on the far side than at the centre, which makes two bulges.
- Pitfalls: Explaining only one bulge and so one tide a day | Expecting high water exactly when the Moon is overhead; coasts and basins delay it by hours | Assuming every coast has two large tides a day. Some ports have one, and many Mediterranean and Baltic tidal ranges are small | Galileo's error: explaining tides by the sloshing of the seas on a moving Earth
- History: greece: c. 325 BC Pytheas links tides and Moon in the Atlantic; c. 150 BC Seleucus of Seleucia; c. 90 BC Posidonius at Cádiz describes the monthly cycle; china: 1st c. AD Wang Chong ties tides to the Moon; 1056 tide table for the Qiantang bore; india: tidal dock at Lothal (c. 2300 BC) is claimed, its function disputed; islamic: 9th c. – Abu Ma'shar's detailed description of lunar tides, influential in Latin translation; europe: 725 Bede notes the fixed delay at each port; 13th c. tide table for London Bridge; 1687 Newton's explanation; 1775 Laplace's dynamic theory; 1872 Kelvin's tide-predicting machine
- Read: Bede, De temporum ratione (725), ch. 29 | David Edgar Cartwright, Tides: A Scientific History (1999)

## The Earth as a magnet `terrestrial_magnetism`
- Deps: needs magnetic_compass
- Core idea: The compass needle points north because the whole Earth is a great magnet, not because of the Pole Star or magnetic mountains. Every magnet has two poles that cannot be separated: break it and each piece has both; like poles repel, unlike attract. A freely pivoted needle lies nearly horizontal at the magnetic equator. Its north-seeking end dips down in the magnetic north and up in the magnetic south. The needle does not point to true north: the deviation (declination) differs from place to place and slowly changes over decades, so charts must record it and navigators check it against the Sun or Pole Star. Iron heated red and cooled or hammered while lying north-south becomes weakly magnetic; heating a magnet red destroys its force.
- Pitfalls: Treating compass north as true north | Claiming garlic or diamonds weaken a magnet (old lore Gilbert tested and refuted) | Hoping to find longitude from declination; it was tried for two centuries and failed | Iron near the compass (guns, nails in the binnacle) falsifies it
- History: china: 1088 – Shen Kuo records that the needle points slightly east of south (declination); thermoremanent 'iron fish' described 1044; europe: 1269 Petrus Peregrinus, letter on the magnet (poles, experiments); c. 1450 declination marked on German sundials; 1581 Norman publishes the dip; 1600 Gilbert, De magnete; 1635 Gellibrand finds declination changes with time; 1701 Halley's chart of declination; 1832–1838 Gauss measures and analyses the field
- Read: William Gilbert, De magnete (1600) | Stephen Pumfrey, Latitude and the Magnetic Earth (2002)

## Deep time - age of the Earth, strata and fossils `deep_time_geology`
- Deps: helped by radioactivity, natural_causes
- Core idea: The Earth is immensely old (about 4.5 thousand million years) and its surface records processes still at work: rain and rivers wear the land down, the debris settles in layers on sea floors, hardens to rock and is later raised and folded into mountains. In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary layers the lower ones are older. Fossils are the remains of real creatures; sea shells on mountains show that the rock was once sea floor. Each group of layers has its own fossils, in the same order everywhere, so rocks can be matched across countries and coal or ore seams followed. Many kinds of animals have died out. Since 1907 the decay of uranium to lead in minerals has given ages in years.
- Pitfalls: Giving the age with no way to show it; before radioactivity only rates of deposition and erosion could be argued, and they gave anything from thousands to hundreds of millions of years | Saying all strata were laid down by one flood | Putting people together with dinosaurs, or mixing up millions and thousands of millions | Ignoring that the claim contradicts the accepted chronology of about 6000 years in Christian and Islamic lands (but not Indian cosmology)
- History: greece: c. 500 BC – Xenophanes takes inland shells and fish imprints as proof of a former sea; islamic: c. 1027 – Ibn Sina, Book of Healing: mountains formed by uplift and erosion over long ages; china: 1088 – Shen Kuo infers shifted coastlines and climate change from fossil shells and petrified bamboo; india: Hindu and Jain cosmology reckons with cycles of thousands of millions of years (not based on rocks); europe: c. 1508 Leonardo's notes on fossils; 1669 Steno's principles of strata; 1788 Hutton; 1796 Cuvier establishes extinction; 1815 William Smith's geological map; 1830–1833 Lyell; 1862 Kelvin's too-short 20–400 million years; 1913 Holmes's radiometric timescale; americas: 1907 Boltwood's first uranium-lead ages; 1956 Patterson: 4.55 thousand million years
- Read: James Hutton, Theory of the Earth, Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1 (1788) | Martin J. S. Rudwick, Earth's Deep History: How It Was Discovered and Why It Matters (2014)

## Continental drift and plate tectonics `plate_tectonics`
- Deps: needs deep_time_geology; helped by world_geography, terrestrial_magnetism
- Core idea: The Earth's outer shell is broken into a dozen rigid plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow, carried by slow flow in the hot rock beneath. Where plates part, new sea floor forms along mid-ocean ridges; where plates converge, one may sink beneath another, forming trenches and volcanic arcs, or two continents may collide and build mountains. Plates also slide past one another along faults. Evidence available early: the coasts of South America and Africa fit, and the same rock formations, fossils and traces of ancient ice continue across the join. Earthquakes and volcanoes lie in narrow belts along plate edges, which tells where they must be expected.
- Pitfalls: Saying continents plough through the ocean floor (Wegener's weak point); the sea floor moves with them | Expecting acceptance on the coastline fit alone; geologists rejected drift until sea-floor evidence in the 1960s | Claiming earthquakes can be predicted to the day | Giving speeds of metres per year
- History: europe: 1596 Ortelius notes the fit of the Atlantic coasts; 1912–1915 Wegener, continental drift; 1929–1931 Holmes proposes mantle convection; 1963 Vine and Matthews, magnetic stripes; americas: 1962 Hess, sea-floor spreading; 1965–1968 Wilson, Morgan and others formulate plate tectonics; africa: 1937 – du Toit (South Africa) assembles the southern-continent evidence
- Read: Alfred Wegener, Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane (1915) | Naomi Oreskes, The Rejection of Continental Drift (1999)

## Stars as suns, galaxies and the expanding universe `stars_galaxies_cosmology`
- Deps: needs heliocentrism; helped by astronomical_distances, spectroscopy, telescope, relativity
- Core idea: The stars are suns, so far away that their light takes years to thousands of years to arrive. The Milky Way is the disc of our own system of some hundred thousand million stars seen from inside; the faint spiral 'nebulae' are other such systems, millions of light years off. Their light is shifted towards the red in proportion to their distance: the universe is expanding and had a hot, dense beginning, now put at about 13.8 thousand million years ago. Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, which is why the Sun can last thousands of millions of years; elements heavier than helium were made in stars.
- Pitfalls: Describing the Big Bang as an explosion into empty space from one point | Stating modern numbers as settled in an era where they were not (Hubble's 1929 scale made the universe younger than the Earth; the term 'Big Bang' dates from 1949, the decisive evidence from 1965) | Saying the Sun burns like a fire | Confusing the solar system, the galaxy and the universe
- History: greece: 5th c. BC – Democritus and Anaxagoras: the Milky Way is the light of many stars; Anaxagoras calls the Sun a glowing stone; islamic: 10th–11th c. – al-Sufi records the Andromeda nebula (964); Ibn al-Haytham and al-Biruni place the Milky Way among the stars; europe: 1584 Bruno: the stars are suns with worlds; 1610 Galileo resolves the Milky Way into stars; 1750–1785 Wright, Kant and Herschel on the Milky Way as a disc; 1927 Lemaître's expanding universe; americas: 1924 Hubble shows Andromeda is a separate galaxy; 1929 distance-redshift law; 1939 Bethe explains stellar fusion; 1965 Penzias and Wilson (Bell Labs) find the cosmic background radiation
- Read: Edwin Hubble, The Realm of the Nebulae (1936) | Simon Singh, Big Bang (2004)

## X-rays (produced in an evacuated tube) `xrays`
- Deps: needs air_pump_vacuum, electromagnetism; helped by photography
- Core idea: When a high voltage from an induction coil is put across a well-evacuated glass tube, the spot where the stream from the negative plate strikes gives off invisible rays that pass through flesh, wood and paper but less through bone and metal. They blacken a wrapped photographic plate and make certain salts glow, so the bones of a living hand or a bullet can be seen. Exposure can cause burns at high doses and increases cancer risk. Limit exposure time, increase distance and use shielding suited to the radiation.
- Pitfalls: No warning about the delayed harm: early workers lost fingers and lives | Tube not evacuated enough or voltage too low: a glow but no X-rays | Confusing X-rays (made by a machine) with radioactivity (from the atom's nucleus)
- History: europe: 1895 Röntgen discovers X-rays (Würzburg), medical use within weeks; 1912 von Laue, X-ray diffraction by crystals; americas: 1913 – Coolidge's hot-cathode X-ray tube
- Read: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, Über eine neue Art von Strahlen (1895) | Abraham Pais, Inward Bound: Of Matter and Forces in the Physical World (1986)

## Radioactivity (spontaneous nuclear decay) `radioactivity`
- Deps: helped by photography, atomic_theory
- Core idea: Uranium and thorium ores give off penetrating rays all the time with no supply of energy, because their atoms break up into atoms of other elements, each isotope having a characteristic half-life: after one half-life, half the original nuclei remain on average. Exposure can cause burns at high doses and increases cancer risk. Limit exposure time, increase distance and use shielding suited to the radiation.
- Pitfalls: No warning about the delayed harm: early workers lost fingers and lives, radium was sold as a tonic and painted on watch dials | Saying radioactivity can be switched off, heated away or is caused by sunlight (Becquerel's first guess) | Confusing X-rays (made by a machine) with radioactivity (from the atom's nucleus)
- History: europe: 1896 Becquerel, rays from uranium; 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie, polonium and radium; 1899–1903 Rutherford and Soddy: alpha and beta rays, transmutation, half-life; americas: 1920s – radium dial painters' poisoning leads to safety rules
- Read: Marie Curie, Recherches sur les substances radioactives (1903) | Abraham Pais, Inward Bound: Of Matter and Forces in the Physical World (1986)

## Structure of the atom (electron, nucleus) `atomic_structure`
- Deps: needs atomic_theory; helped by air_pump_vacuum, electromagnetism, radioactivity, periodic_table, spectroscopy
- Core idea: Atoms are not indivisible. Each has a tiny, heavy, positively charged nucleus, about a hundred-thousandth of the atom's width but holding nearly all its mass, surrounded by very light negative electrons; the rest is empty. The number of positive charges (protons) in the nucleus fixes which element it is and its place in the periodic table; neutrons add weight without charge, giving varieties (isotopes) of the same element. Chemistry and electric current are the business of the outer electrons alone. Evidence: the cathode stream in an evacuated tube is bent by magnets and consists of particles about 1800 times lighter than a hydrogen atom, the same from every metal; and when alpha rays are shot at thin gold foil, most pass straight through but about one in several thousand bounces back.
- Pitfalls: Teaching the little solar system as literal truth; orbiting electrons would radiate and fall in, which is what quantum theory had to resolve | Saying the nucleus contains electrons (the accepted view until the neutron was found in 1932) | Mixing up atom, molecule and nucleus, or atomic weight and atomic number | Offering it to an era with no means to test it and no use for it
- History: europe: 1897 J. J. Thomson identifies the electron; 1909 Geiger and Marsden's gold-foil scattering; 1911 Rutherford's nucleus; 1913 Bohr's model, Moseley's atomic numbers, Soddy's isotopes; 1919 Aston's mass spectrograph; 1932 Chadwick's neutron; americas: 1909–1913 – Millikan measures the electron's charge; east_asia: 1904 – Nagaoka (Japan) proposes a 'Saturnian' atom with a massive centre
- Read: Ernest Rutherford, The Scattering of α and β Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom, Philosophical Magazine 21 (1911) | Abraham Pais, Inward Bound: Of Matter and Forces in the Physical World (1986)

## Quantum mechanics `quantum_mechanics`
- Deps: needs atomic_structure, wave_nature_light_sound; helped by spectroscopy, periodic_table, heat_energy_conservation
- Core idea: On the scale of atoms, energy comes in fixed packets. Light of frequency f is taken up and given out only in quanta of energy h times f (h is Planck's constant), and electrons in an atom can have only certain energies, which is why each element shows sharp spectral lines and why atoms are stable. Electrons and all particles also behave as waves, with wavelength h divided by momentum, and the theory predicts only probabilities; position and momentum cannot both be sharp. No two electrons can occupy the same state, which builds up the shells behind the periodic table and explains metals, insulators and semiconductors. What convinces: for a surface whose threshold lies between red and violet, faint violet light can release electrons while brighter red light cannot in the single-photon regime; the hydrogen spectrum is calculated to many digits; electrons bounced off a nickel crystal make a diffraction pattern like X-rays (Davisson and Germer, Bell Labs, 1927).
- Pitfalls: Slogans without content ('everything is uncertain', 'the observer's mind creates reality') | Using it to justify mysticism, telepathy or free will | Presenting Schrödinger's cat as a real effect rather than his objection | Being unable to give one number or one experiment; a layperson can honestly convey E = h f, discrete levels and electron diffraction, but not the mathematics | Describing electrons as small balls on definite orbits
- History: europe: 1900 Planck's quantum for heat radiation; 1905 Einstein's light quanta; 1913 Bohr's atom; 1924 de Broglie's matter waves; 1925–1927 Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Born, Dirac: the full theory, uncertainty relation; 1925 Pauli's exclusion principle; india: 1924 – Bose's statistics of light quanta; americas: 1916 Millikan confirms the photoelectric law; 1923 Compton effect; 1927 Davisson and Germer, electron diffraction; 1947 the transistor as an application of the quantum theory of solids
- Read: George Gamow, Thirty Years that Shook Physics (1966) | Richard P. Feynman, QED: The Strange Theory of Light and Matter (1985) | Manjit Kumar, Quantum: Einstein, Bohr and the Great Debate about the Nature of Reality (2008)

## Relativity (special and general) `relativity`
- Deps: needs laws_of_motion, speed_of_light; helped by electromagnetism, universal_gravitation, wave_nature_light_sound
- Core idea: The speed of light in empty space is the same for every observer, however the source or observer moves, and nothing can go faster. It follows that time and length are not absolute: a clock moving past at speed v runs slow by the factor square root of (1 - v²/c²), unnoticeable at everyday speeds (at a tenth of light speed half a per cent), and events simultaneous for one observer are not for another. Mass and energy are equivalent, E = m c²: a gram of matter corresponds to the heat of burning some 3000 tonnes of coal. General relativity treats gravity as the curvature of space and time by mass: clocks run slower lower down, and light passing the Sun is bent. What convinced by the 1940s: the failure to detect the Earth's motion through an ether (Michelson and Morley, 1887); the unexplained 43 seconds of arc per century in Mercury's orbit; starlight bent by 1.75 seconds of arc at the 1919 eclipse; fast electrons growing harder to deflect; cosmic-ray particles living longer in flight (1941); and the energy balance of nuclear reactions (1932).
- Pitfalls: Summing it up as 'everything is relative'; the theory is about what stays the same | Saying E = m c² is the recipe for the bomb; it is the bookkeeping, fission is the mechanism | Saying Einstein received the Nobel Prize for relativity (it was for the photoelectric effect) | Muddling the twin story, or claiming speeds simply add up beyond that of light | Offering it before Maxwell's electromagnetism and precise optics exist, when it solves no known problem
- History: europe: 1889–1904 FitzGerald, Lorentz, Poincaré: contraction and transformation formulas; 1905 Einstein, special relativity and E = m c²; 1908 Minkowski's space-time; 1915 general relativity; 1919 Eddington's eclipse expeditions (Príncipe and Sobral); 1932 Cockcroft and Walton verify the mass-energy balance; americas: 1887 Michelson and Morley’s null result in Cleveland. 1938 Ives and Stilwell measure time dilation; 1941 Rossi and Hall, lifetime of fast mesotrons (muons)
- Read: Albert Einstein, Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper, Annalen der Physik 17 (1905) | Albert Einstein, Über die spezielle und die allgemeine Relativitätstheorie (1917) | Abraham Pais, Subtle is the Lord: The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein (1982)

## Nuclear fission and the chain reaction `nuclear_fission`
- Deps: needs atomic_structure, radioactivity; helped by relativity, periodic_table
- Core idea: A uranium nucleus can split after absorbing a neutron, producing two lighter nuclei, heat and further neutrons. The discovery hinged on chemistry: Hahn and Strassmann found barium among the products of irradiated uranium. Meitner and Frisch explained how splitting a heavy nucleus could release so much energy. If one fission leads on average to one further fission, the reaction continues at a steady rate. Reactor operators can adjust neutron absorption to regulate the rate. Radioactive fission products continue to release heat even after the chain reaction has stopped. The first human-made reactor sustained a controlled chain reaction in Chicago in December 1942.
- Pitfalls: Assuming every neutron that enters uranium causes fission. Some scatter or are absorbed without splitting a nucleus | Confusing fission, the splitting of a heavy nucleus, with fusion, the joining of light nuclei | Assuming that stopping a chain reaction immediately stops heat production or makes irradiated material safe | Explaining the release of energy as an ordinary chemical reaction. The change is in nuclear binding energy
- History: europe: 1932 Chadwick's neutron; 1933–1934 Szilard conceives and patents a neutron chain reaction; 1934 Fermi's neutron bombardment of uranium (Rome), Ida Noddack's ignored suggestion of splitting; December 1938 Hahn and Strassmann find barium (Berlin); January 1939 Meitner and Frisch explain and name fission; 1939 Joliot's group shows surplus neutrons; 1940 Frisch–Peierls memorandum on a fast-neutron bomb; americas: 1939 Bohr and Wheeler's theory; 2 December 1942 first human-made self-sustaining reactor (Chicago Pile-1); 16 July 1945 Trinity test; August 1945 Smyth Report makes the outline public; east_asia: August 1945 – Hiroshima and Nagasaki; africa: 1972 – isotope measurements identify evidence of natural fission reactors at Oklo in Gabon, active about two thousand million years ago
- Read: Lise Meitner & Otto R. Frisch, Disintegration of Uranium by Neutrons: a New Type of Nuclear Reaction, Nature 143 (1939) | Henry DeWolf Smyth, Atomic Energy for Military Purposes (1945) | Richard Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)
